title: Remove Duplicates, Keep Order
oneLiner: Keep the first copy of each value in its original order, using a set to remember what you've already seen.
keyTakeaway: A set alone loses the order; a list alone makes every "seen it?" check O(n). Use both: the set answers membership in O(1) and the output list keeps the order, for O(n) overall.
explanation:
Return a new list with duplicates removed, keeping the first occurrence of each value and the original order: [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] gives [3, 1, 2].

Turning the list into a set removes duplicates but loses the order (sets have no positions), so on its own it fails the tests. Checking result.Contains(x) or x in result before appending keeps the order but searches the output list each time, O(n) per check and O(n²) overall. The standard answer uses both structures: a set of values seen so far, and the output list. For each value, if it isn't in the set, add it to the set and append it to the output. In C#, HashSet.Add returns false when the value was already there, so if (seen.Add(x)) result.Add(x); does both in one line.

Shortcuts exist: nums.Distinct().ToList() in C# (which keeps first occurrences in order in practice, though its documentation doesn't promise it) and list(dict.fromkeys(nums)) in Python (dictionaries keep insertion order). Write the set version first; it's the one that carries over to harder problems.

complexity.note: One pass with an O(1) average set check per element; the set and the output hold up to n values. Checking the output list instead of a set would make it O(n²).
